noteBlocks.md:
**The pill and the implant** change hormone levels, so **no ovum develops** — link 1 never happens.
**Male sterilisation** cuts the **sperm tubes**, so sperm cannot leave.
**The condom** is a **barrier**, so sperm never reach the ovum.
**Female sterilisation** cuts the **oviducts**, so the ovum and the sperm cannot meet.

Name the link and you have the mechanism. That is what the marks are for.

noteBlocks.title: Why the grouping matters more than it looks
noteBlocks.md:
CCEA sorts contraception into **mechanical**, **chemical** and **surgical**. Almost every revision site sorts it into *hormonal* and *non-hormonal* instead, because that is how the other boards teach it.

The two groupings cut across each other: a condom and sterilisation are both *non-hormonal*, and CCEA calls one **mechanical** and the other **surgical**. Use CCEA's three words on the answer line.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "Contraception"
noteBlocks.why: A quick second pass over the methods, now that you have the chain to hang them on. It is made for another board, so it sorts them into hormonal and non-hormonal — translate each one back into CCEA's three groups as you watch, and the question underneath asks you to do exactly that.

noteBlocks.title: Two things to let pass in that clip
noteBlocks.md: Clips made for the other boards name methods CCEA does not — **coils**, **patches**, **injections**, **diaphragms**, **spermicides** — and they usually give the pill's mechanism as **inhibiting FSH**. FSH is not on this specification at all, and the wording CCEA marks is **changes hormone levels**. Keep to the four methods and the three groups above.

noteBlocks.prompt: CCEA sorts contraception into three groups. A condom belongs to the ______ group.
noteBlocks.explain: Mechanical, because it works as a physical barrier. The pill and the implant are chemical; sterilisation is surgical.

noteBlocks.text: 3. The one thing only a barrier can do

noteBlocks.credit: Dr Elena Kontogianni, Wikimedia Commons, CC0

noteBlocks.md:
A condom stops something **passing between two people**. So it is the only method here that also prevents the spread of **sexually transmitted infections** — **HIV**, which leads to AIDS, and **chlamydia**, which can cause **infertility** if it is left untreated.

The pill changes what happens inside **one** body, so it cannot do that. If a question asks for an advantage of a condom over the pill, this is the answer it wants.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which advantage does a condom have that the contraceptive pill does not?
options: it helps to prevent sexually transmitted infections
it is more reliable at preventing pregnancy
noteBlocks.answer: it helps to prevent sexually transmitted infections
noteBlocks.explain: Only a barrier stops an infection passing between partners. On the survey data the pill is in fact the more reliable of the two at preventing pregnancy.

noteBlocks.title: Worked example: 'Explain how taking the contraceptive pill stops a pregnancy starting. [2]'
noteBlocks.md:
**Step 1 — find the link it breaks.** The pill acts on link 1, before an ovum has developed. Locating the cut stops you writing a barrier answer.
**Step 2 — first half.** It **changes hormone levels**. **[1]**
**Step 3 — second half.** So **no ovum develops or is released**. **[1]**
**Step 4 — check.** Nothing about blocking or killing sperm.

A mechanism answer always needs the cause **and** the consequence.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the survey shown, 70 of 1000 women using the contraceptive pill became pregnant in a year. What percentage is that?
noteBlocks.explain: 70 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 7.0%. Most of those failures are missed doses rather than the drug failing.

noteBlocks.md:
Causes of infertility include a **lack of sperm**, sperm **without flagella**, **blocked oviducts**, a **lack of ova** and a **lack of the right hormones**.

Treatment, in the specification's own words: **hormones to produce multiple ova**, **in vitro fertilisation**, and the **transfer of several embryos into the uterus**.

parts.stem:
A couple are choosing between the condom, the contraceptive pill and sterilisation.
Describe how each of these three methods prevents pregnancy. Then weigh the condom against the pill, giving one point in the condom's favour and one against it.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: the condom is a mechanical method: a barrier that stops sperm reaching the ovum
the contraceptive pill is a chemical method: it changes hormone levels
so no ovum develops or is released
sterilisation is a surgical method: the sperm tubes or the oviducts are cut
an advantage of the condom: it also stops sexually transmitted infections such as HIV and chlamydia passing between partners
a disadvantage of the condom: it can tear or be used wrongly, so it is less reliable than the pill
a decision that names the couple's own situation

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Band A needs both halves of the question: the three mechanisms and a real comparison of the condom with the pill. An answer that describes the methods but never compares them caps at Band B. Two losses recur in the reports: the pill described as a barrier, and an 'advantage' given as effectiveness, which on the data is the pill's advantage rather than the condom's. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Take the three methods in turn, and give each one its CCEA group: mechanical, chemical or surgical.
For the comparison, one clear advantage and one clear disadvantage, each with a reason.
parts.workedSolution: The condom is a mechanical method. It is a barrier, so the sperm cannot reach the ovum. The contraceptive pill is a chemical method: it changes hormone levels, and that stops an ovum developing so none is released. Sterilisation is a surgical method: in a man the sperm tubes are cut so sperm cannot leave, and in a woman the oviducts are cut so the ovum and sperm cannot meet. The condom has one advantage nothing else on this list has: it also stops sexually transmitted infections such as HIV and chlamydia passing between partners. Its disadvantage is that it can tear or be used wrongly, so it is less reliable than the pill, which for a couple who are certain they do not want a pregnancy may matter more.

pattern.regex: \bpill\b(?![^.;\n]{0,40}(is not|isnt|never) a barrier)[^.;\n]{0,40}(barrier|blocks? the sperm|stops? the sperm reaching)

commonErrors.feedback: The pill is not a barrier. It changes hormone levels inside one body so that no ovum develops; only a barrier stops something passing between two people.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Of the 1250 treatment cycles started by women under 35, 400 ended in a live birth. Calculate the percentage that ended in a live birth. [2]'
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is the right rule. Line 2 uses the wrong whole: 850 is the number of cycles that did NOT end in a live birth. The whole is every cycle started, successes included, which is 1250.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the two: the rule in line 1 stands. The habit that catches this is to ask what the parts add up to — 400 live births and 850 without add to 1250, and that total is always the denominator.

prompts.prompt: How does the contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
prompts.answer: It changes hormone levels, and that stops an ovum developing so none is released.

prompts.prompt: Name CCEA's three groups of contraception and give one method in each.
prompts.answer: Mechanical: the condom. Chemical: the contraceptive pill, or an implant. Surgical: sterilisation.

prompts.prompt: What can a condom do that the contraceptive pill cannot?
prompts.answer: A condom also prevents the spread of sexually transmitted infections, such as HIV and chlamydia, because only a barrier stops something passing between two people.

prompts.prompt: Which tube is cut in male sterilisation, and which in female sterilisation?
prompts.answer: The sperm tubes are cut in male sterilisation, so sperm cannot leave. The oviducts are cut in female sterilisation, so the ovum and the sperm cannot meet.

prompts.prompt: Describe in vitro fertilisation in three steps, as the specification states it. (Higher Tier)
prompts.answer: Hormones are used to produce multiple ova; the ova are fertilised in a dish in the laboratory; and several embryos are transferred into the uterus.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for an ethical reason why someone might not use contraception. What kind of answer earns the mark?
prompts.answer: A religious or moral reason: something the person believes to be right or wrong. Cost, side effects and reliability are practical reasons, not ethical ones.
